newsitem.title: USA: NYS voters split on ending rent rules - survey.
newsitem.headline: NYS voters split on ending rent rules - survey.

text.p: New York State voters split on a controversial plan to end rent controls for apartments, though most would support making it harder for high-income earners to qualify, a new survey showed on Thursday.

New York State Senator Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, has proposed a controversial plan to end rent rules, while keeping protections for the needy, disabled and elderly. The battle over rent rules, which the Democrat-led Assembly, wants permanently extended, has become a major obstacle towards getting a state budget approved.

By a 56 percent to 33 percent, voters support lowering the rent regulation ceiling, so that a household that earns more than $100,000 and pays more than $2,000 a month in rent would not qualify. In New York City, which has the lion's share of rent regulated apartments, this idea was approved by a 52 to 39 percent margin.

Eliminating rent rules could have a considerable impact: 60 percent of the 917 New Yorkers who identified themselves as registered voters said "many" people would be forced to move, while 25 percent said "some" would have to.
Overall, 48 percent of the group favored continuing the current laws, but 44 percent think they should be ended, either by being phased out--33 percent--or ended now--11 percent.
And most New Yorkers--53 to 42 percent--want government involved in setting apartment rents.

"Maybe upstate and suburban voters don't like New York City, but our poll suggests they like landlords even less," said Maurice Carroll, the director of the institute, in prepared remarks. "Tenant groups have argued that the cost of housing in New York City is a serious problem and that many New Yorkers would be forced to move if rent regulations are ended. Quinnipiac College finds most voters agree."
The survey, which was conducted from April 14 to 20, has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percent.
